title: The problem: missing babies
plain_summary: About 2.3 million newborns died worldwide in 2023. Tanzania's 2022/23 survey put its newborn death rate at 24 per 1,000 live births, about 48,000 deaths a year, and the country is off track for the global 2030 goal of fewer than 12 per 1,000.

title: What the researchers did
plain_summary: They pulled newborn-death records from DHIS2, Tanzania's national health data system, for 28 regional referral hospitals and 7 tertiary hospitals over 2015-2024, then tested the data three ways: is it complete, is it internally consistent, and is it plausible against national surveys.

title: Are hospitals even reporting?
plain_summary: Across all facilities, hospitals filed newborn-death reports in only 58.3% of the months they were supposed to. Regional hospitals did a little better than tertiary hospitals, but none of the 7 tertiary hospitals reported in more than 73% of months.

title: Do the numbers hold together?
plain_summary: Only about 29% of hospitals reported newborn death rates that stayed internally consistent year to year (within WHO's plus-or-minus 33% band). Many facilities swung wildly or dropped out entirely for months.

title: Do the numbers match reality?
plain_summary: The system's newborn death rate for 2024 was just 5.9 per 1,000 (adjusted), while the national survey said 24 and UN estimates said 21. The routine system is missing more than three quarters of the deaths.

title: A second opinion: DHIS2 vs NID
plain_summary: For seven hospitals, researchers compared DHIS2 against NEST360's detailed newborn database (NID). Three regional hospitals reported higher rates in DHIS2 than NID; one tertiary hospital matched closely in later years.

title: What it means and what to fix
plain_summary: Undercounting hides where babies are dying and weakens decisions. Fixes include letting DHIS2 record real zeros, assigning staff to enter data, moving to individual-level records, and linking data systems. None of these cost much.
